newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine economy seen unmoved by Kuchma reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine economy seen unmoved by Kuchma reshuffle.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma has sacked four ministers with economic and financial portfolios in a move analysts said was unlikely to improve the country's troubled economy.
"It's senseless. The big problems lie in the economy and a reshuffle won't change a thing," said Olexander Razumkov, head of the Centre for Independent Political and Economic Studies.
Top of the list was Finance Minister Valentyn Koronevsky, dismissed on Tuesday for what Kuchma's press service said were "serious inadequacies in his work" .
Next came Statistics Minister Olexander Osaulenko, sacked for bad management.
Economy Minister Vasyl Hureyev and the minister for machine-building and the military complex, Valery Maleyev, were moved to other, unspecified posts.
"It is a last-ditch attempt to get the ship on course, but it's a waste of time. It's the middle people who are slowing things up," said a Western economist who asked not to be named.
Analysts saw the move as an attempt to silence critics and possibly to save Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, whose criticism of the ministers last Friday appeared to spark the clean-out.
"It may be a pre-emptive strike by Lazarenko to protect his own position," one analyst said. "If Lazarenko goes, the whole system will collapse," said another.
Analysts said the sackings were unlikely to have any major impact on economic policy, controlled by Kuchma, Lazarenko and Viktor Pynzenyk, deputy prime minister in charge of reform.

Kuchma was due to interrupt his holiday in western Ukraine to meet Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and potential Italian investors on Wednesday and his absence from Kiev lent weight to the idea Lazarenko was seeking to look in control.
The sackings shocked no one, as Kuchma has said repeatedly that ministerial changes were necessary.
There was no official word on who would replace the four, but reformist deputy Sergei Teryokhin said Ihor Mityukov, a former deputy finance minister, could take over from Koronevsky.
He quoted "reliable government sources" as saying he was one of four men who had flown to see Kuchma earlier on Tuesday.
Following that theory, State Property Fund Chairman Yuri Yekhanurov would become economy minister and Hureyev would move to the machine-building ministry, Teryokhin said.
Kuchma launched the reshuffle this month when he sacked his agriculture minister and deputy transport minister at the first meeting of a new anti-corruption body.

The government, and Lazarenko himself, have come under fire from conservatives for unpaid wages, liberals for not reforming enough and industrialists who say a new package of tax laws fails to support domestic producers.
The laws could face several votes in parliament, which has been slow to address them since they were presented in November.

Kuchma and reformers in the former Soviet republic of 52 million want the new laws to be passed to pave the way for a new $2.5-$3 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund, attract more foreign investment and improve tax collection.
The new tax reform package would also scrap the system of "kartoteka" where enterprises can legally avoid paying taxes by officially declaring they have no funds.
Pynzenyk has blamed kartoteka for much of a shadow economy estimated by experts at between 40 and 50 percent of output.
Kuchma's most obvious problem as far as most Ukrainians are concerned is a mountain of unpaid wages and pensions which has brought miners, teachers and students onto the streets.

Non-payments stood at 4.2 billion hryvnias ($2.3 billion) at the start of the year from three billion hryvnias in the middle of last year. Gross domestic product fell by 10.4 percent in January year-on-year. $ = 1.8150 hryvnias
